extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (patent/trademark practitioners, OED, and disciplinary judges)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules applied in USPTO disciplinary proceedings addressing practitioner conduct before the USPTO (signing rules, client communications, fee divisions, cooperation with investigations, burden of proof, sanctions factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO disciplinary authority (35 U.S.C. §§2(b)(2)(D) and 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before the Office; 35 U.S.C. §32 empowers the USPTO to discipline a practitioner who is shown to be incompetent, disreputable, guilty of gross misconduct, or who violates USPTO regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary hearings follow 37 C.F.R. part 11 subpart C and section 7 of the APA (5 U.S.C. §556); practitioners must receive notice and opportunity for a hearing; authority supports issuance of exclusionary sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of notice and opportunity for hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must receive notice and an opportunity for a hearing before disciplinary action is taken (35 U.S.C. §32; 37 C.F.R. part 11; 5 U.S.C. §556).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures are conducted by hearing officers appointed to hear USPTO cases; failure to provide such process would violate the statute and APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failure to answer Complaint (37 C.F.R. §11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent does not file an answer or otherwise participate, the Court may deem the allegations admitted and enter default judgment and sanctions (including exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. §11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director bears the burden of proving alleged disciplinary violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence requires a level of proof between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt; evidence must produce a firm belief or conviction in the trier of fact and be certain, unambiguous, and persuasive (cases cited: Johnson; Addington; Jimenez; Foster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to respond to Requests for Information (RFIs) (37 C.F.R. §11.22(f)(1)(ii); 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner has an ethical obligation to respond to any lawfully issued RFI from OED; failure to respond to RFIs can be the basis for discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RFIs are lawfully issued under the cited rules; multiple RFIs, lack-of-response letters, final notices, and requests to correspond electronically must be answered within specified timeframes or consequences follow (disciplinary charges and use as basis for aggravation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature requirements (37 C.F.R. §2.193(a),(c); TMEP §611.01(b),(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of correspondence that requires a signature must bear either a handwritten signature personally signed by the person named as the signatory or an electronic signature personally entered by that person; electronic signatures must be personally entered and placed between forward slashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DIRECT sign method (named signatory personally enters signature) is default; E SIGN-ON and H SIGN-ON are alternatives but the person named must personally sign; typing another person’s electronic signature or signature of another person is not a valid signature; TMEP clarifies that paralegals/assistants may not sign for attorneys or authorized signatories.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS/TICRS evidence of signature method and IP address
rubrics_metrics.description: TICRS captures when a document is created and submitted via TEAS, the signature method used, the filing receipt email, and the IP address of the computer used to access TEAS; when DIRECT is used, the IP address reflects approximate geographic location of the signer’s computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TICRS and TEAS data can establish who entered signatures, where signing activity originated, and timing—useful evidence of impermissible signatures and patterns of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on others signing for named signatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, secretary) may not sign the name of an attorney or other authorized signatory on USPTO trademark filings; typing another’s electronic signature is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where an electronic signature method exists, the named signatory must personally enter the signature elements; impersonation or delegation without authorization violates signature rules and can lead to discipline and jeopardize applications (declarations signed under 18 U.S.C. §1001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. §11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to ensure trademark filings were signed in accordance with USPTO rules, or failing to supervise staff and affiliates to ensure compliance, constitutes a violation of this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. §11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to inform clients about actual or potential adverse consequences of noncompliance with signature rules, or failures to provide updates, violates this duty and is an ethical breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to explain matters to permit informed decisions (37 C.F.R. §11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must explain the legal and practical consequences (e.g., jeopardy to applications/registrations) of impermissible signing practices so clients can decide whether to take action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of fees with non-firm practitioners (37 C.F.R. §11.105(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Division of a fee between practitioners not in the same firm may only be made if division is in proportion to services performed, the client agrees to the arrangement confirmed in writing, and the total fee is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to obtain written client consent, to disclose the division and shares, or to ensure proportionality and reasonableness violates the rule and can be a basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor to tribunal; prohibition on false statements (37 C.F.R. §11.303(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing trademark applications that imply the named signatory actually signed, and failing to correct that implied falsehood after learning of impermissible signatures, violates this duty to the tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on offering known false evidence; remedial measures (37 C.F.R. §11.303(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly offer evidence the practitioner knows to be false; if material evidence offered is later known to be false, the practitioner must take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner discovers falsity in filed declarations, they must take steps (including disclosure) to remedy the situation; withholding or ignoring falsity is disciplinary misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose adverse material facts to tribunal and clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have obligations to disclose adverse material facts to the tribunal or clients when necessary as part of remedial measures and client communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to disclose impermissible signing practices to the USPTO or to affected clients violates ethical duties, harms the integrity of the registry, and aggravates sanction considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiduciary duty to clients
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner owes a fiduciary duty of implicit confidence and trust to clients, acting with devotion to clients’ interests and exerting utmost learning and ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions that deprive clients of information, expose their rights to jeopardy, or otherwise betray confidence violate the fiduciary duty and are weighty ethical breaches for sanctioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to cooperate with disciplinary investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: During an OED investigation, a practitioner must respond to lawful requests for information and cooperate; failure to do so violates USPTO rules (and 37 C.F.R. §11.801(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated failures to respond to RFIs, lack-of-response letters, and final notices can be charged as misconduct and are aggravating when imposing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental state analysis for discipline (intentional, knowing, negligent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer’s mental state at the time of misconduct (intentional, knowing, or negligent) determines culpability and influences appropriate discipline; intent is most culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent = conscious objective to accomplish result; knowing = conscious awareness of nature/circumstances; these mental states justify more severe sanctions than negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm criterion: actual or potential injury suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: The harm resulting from misconduct need not be actual; potential injury to clients, the tribunal, or the public suffices to justify significant sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include jeopardy to trademark applications/registrations and harm to registry integrity; number of affected clients and potential for cancellation increase severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider listed aggravating and mitigating factors when fashioning sanctions (e.g., absence of prior record as mitigation; aggravators include dishonest/selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, multiple violations, bad faith obstruction, failure to cooperate, refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing, substantial experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of multiple aggravating factors (dishonesty, pattern, multiple offenses, obstruction, lack of remorse, experience) supports more severe sanctions such as exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of misconduct and multiple offenses as aggravating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated instances of similar misconduct and committing multiple offenses in a single proceeding are aggravating factors that warrant harsher discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple violations affecting multiple clients and different rules (e.g., 22 separate provisions) support heightened sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad faith obstruction of disciplinary proceedings as aggravator
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders of the disciplinary agency (e.g., not filing an answer, not seeking permission to file late) constitutes bad faith obstruction and is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to participate in the disciplinary process demonstrates contempt for procedures and supports enhanced discipline, including exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing / lack of remorse as aggravator
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to acknowledge the wrongful nature of conduct or absence of remorse is an aggravating factor warranting more severe sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing no remorse or boasting about evading discipline (e.g., claiming residence precludes USPTO action) increases sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal recognition limits for foreign practitioners (37 C.F.R. §11.14(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal recognition granted to foreign trademark agents is limited (e.g., to representing parties located in the agent’s country of admission) and requires compliance with USPTO rules of professional conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner granted limited recognition must conform to applicable USPTO rules and cannot represent applicants located outside permitted scope (violations of scope can be charged).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of declarations signed under penalty (18 U.S.C. §1001)
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations in many trademark filings contain certifications signed under criminal penalty pursuant to 18 U.S.C. §1001, making false or improperly signed declarations especially serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper signatures on declarations expose practitioners and clients to potential criminal and civil consequences and heighten the ethical breach.
